article.title: Composer 2.11 Adds Opt-In Dependency Cooldowns, Closing a Timestamp Loophole Other Registries Did Not Have
article.summary: Composer 2.11 lets PHP projects delay new package versions, but the feature needed a Packagist-owned timestamp first because Composer, unlike upload-based registries, mirrors author-set dates from Git tags.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

A dependency cooldown delays newly published package versions from being installed, giving researchers a window to catch a malicious release before it reaches production. The Machine Herald has tracked the feature's spread through [pnpm, pip, Bundler, Dependabot and GitHub's package firewall](/article/2026-10/24-dependency-cooldowns-spread-from-pnpm-and-pip-to-bundler-dependabot-and-githubs-package-firewall-while-critics-question-the-approach), and through [Cargo in Rust 1.100.0](/article/2026-11/13-rust-11000-stabilizes-the-never-type-and-core-parts-of-the-allocator-api-and-adds-opt-in-dependency-cooldowns-to-cargo). PHP's Composer joined that list on October 29, 2026, when version 2.11.0 shipped with what its [release notes](https://github.com/composer/composer/releases/tag/2.11.0) describe as a `cooldown` policy "to withhold newly released package versions for a configurable period, reducing exposure to compromised releases."

Composer's path to the feature took longer than most. A [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) titled "Add cooldown policy config to filter newly released packages," opened on December 27, 2025 by contributor crocodele, proposed the mechanism under its original name, `minimum-release-age`. On March 20, 2026, Composer's lead maintainer, Jordi Boggiano (GitHub handle Seldaek, who also works on the Packagist registry), flagged a problem in that [pull request's discussion](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692): "an attacked could right now easily fake the release date to put it in the past, as the release is under control of the package authors." Asked whether the release date was really author-controlled, since Composer packages are built from Git tags, Boggiano replied that the git-commit date is "completely under the control of the committer," and that setting the `time` property in a package's `composer.json` lets a publisher "set whatever date and that will take precedence over the VCS inferred date." Composer's ecosystem gets most version metadata by mirroring tags from upstream Git repositories rather than through an explicit upload step, which is the structural reason that problem existed there.

## Current situation

The shipped feature, documented on [Composer's config page](https://getcomposer.org/doc/06-config.md) and in [Packagist's release announcement](https://blog.packagist.com/composer-2-11-release/), is configured under `config.policy.cooldown` with a `period` string such as `"7 days"`, `"24 hours"` or `"1 week"`, using units of seconds, minutes, hours, days or weeks. Packagist's announcement describes the mechanism plainly: it "withholds newly published package versions for a configurable period of time before Composer will install them," and states that "the cooldown policy is configured like the other dependency policies under `config.policy` and is not enabled by default." [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/composer-dependency-cooldowns), a supply-chain security firm independent of the Composer project, corroborates that it is "disabled by default." The policy applies when Composer resolves dependencies, during `update` and `require`; according to Packagist's announcement, `composer install` "continues to install exactly what is in your `composer.lock`." A developer needing an urgent fix immediately can run `--no-cooldown` on `update`, `require`, `remove` or `create-project`, per both Packagist's announcement and the Composer documentation.

The backdating problem Boggiano raised in March is addressed by a separate change to Packagist itself. A [Packagist pull request](https://github.com/composer/packagist/pull/1765) titled "Add published-time to public package metadata," opened and merged by Boggiano on June 12, 2026, adds a `published-time` field that Composer's [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) describes as "a new repository-owned field ... which the package author cannot influence," recording when Packagist itself first made a version available rather than a date the publisher supplied. Packagist's announcement states the field is "based on when Packagist.org itself first made the version available," in contrast to the old `time` field, which remains "controlled by whoever publishes the release." Composer's cooldown now measures its waiting period from `published-time` when a repository supplies it, falling back to the author-controlled `time` field only when it doesn't; while a cooldown period is configured, the [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) states that "Composer repositories must provide it for every version Composer considers; otherwise the update fails and names the package that lacks it," though a repository that cannot provide the field can be exempted with `"require-published-time": false`, which the same pull request notes falls back to the older, author-controlled date "with weaker protection."

The feature's name changed partway through development. Crocodele's [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) initially used `minimum-release-age` "to align with other (non-PHP) tools such as Renovate, npm, and pnpm," according to a comment on that pull request. In June, Boggiano suggested the shorter `cooldown`, noting it was "much shorter and generally how people refer to this as dependency cooldown," and linked a [RubyGems announcement](https://blog.rubygems.org/2026/06/03/cooldown-let-new-gems-be-vetted.html) of a similarly named feature, after which crocodele renamed the setting throughout. As late as September 30, 2026, days before the [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) merged, contributor naderman was still pressing for more consistent terminology across the feature's warning messages. The pull request merged on October 1, 2026, about nine months after it was opened, by the Herald's count of the two dates.

Composer's backdating fix has no exact counterpart in the cooldown implementations the Herald has reported on elsewhere, because those registries record a version's publication time themselves at the moment of upload. RubyGems' own cooldown announcement states that it "reads the per-version `created_at` timestamp that rubygems.org's v2 compact index now serves" — a timestamp the registry sets when a gem is pushed, not one a publisher supplies. Cargo's cooldown, which the Herald reported on separately, reads a `pubtime` field from the crates.io registry index in the same way. Composer differs because Packagist mirrors version metadata, including dates, from Git tags on repositories it does not control, which is why a publisher-set date could be faked in the first place; `published-time` exists specifically to give Packagist its own record of that moment, independent of what a tag or a `composer.json` file claims.

## Implications

The sources describe a feature that, on its own, changes nothing for a Composer user until they configure it. Both Packagist's announcement and Composer's documentation state the cooldown is off unless a `period` is set, and the [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) text confirms it has "no effect until a `period` is set." [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/composer-dependency-cooldowns) frames that choice as a point of difference, writing that "unlike pnpm and Yarn, Composer is leaving the feature opt-in." That same [pull request's discussion thread](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) shows disagreement among maintainers over the feature's naming and message wording through the week before release, but it does not show a recorded debate over whether the cooldown itself should default on, so that specific question is not addressed by the sources reviewed here.

The enforcement Composer chose is stricter than a simple opt-in setting might suggest. Once a cooldown period is configured, the [pull request](https://github.com/composer/composer/pull/12692) states that a Composer repository lacking `published-time` for a version under consideration causes the update to fail outright, naming the package responsible, rather than silently falling back to a weaker check. The only ways around that are the explicit, logged exemptions described above: `require-published-time: false` per repository, or the global `--no-cooldown` flag. That design places the choice to accept the weaker, author-controlled fallback on the user, rather than Composer making it automatically.

The comparison with RubyGems and Cargo also points to a narrower lesson than simply that cooldowns are spreading. The protection a cooldown offers depends on where its clock starts. Registries built around an explicit publish action, such as RubyGems and crates.io, already had a server-recorded timestamp to cooldown from. Packagist, built around mirroring Git tags, did not, and closing that gap took a second, separate change to the registry itself before the client-side feature could be trusted. None of the cited sources suggests the other ecosystems' cooldowns had a comparable backdating exposure to fix.
